source_text: Hunc igitur agnoscimus et scimus deum, conditorem rerum omnium, dominum, propter potestatem, et parentem propter institutionem: hunc inquam, qui dzx7t, et facta sunt omnia; praecepit, et processerunt uniuersa; de quo scriptum est: omnia in sapientia fecisti; de quo Moyses: deus in caelo sursum et in terra deorsum; qui secundum Isaiam mensus est caelum palmo, terram pugillo: qui aspicit terram, et facit eam tremere: qui continet gyrum terrae, et eos qui habitant in ipso quasi locustae: qui expendit montes in pondere, et nemora in statera, id est certo diuinae dispositionis examine: ac, ne facile in ruinam procumberet magnitudo inaequaliter iacens, si non paribus fuisset librata ponderibus, onus hoc moderanter terrenae molis aequauit. qui dicit per prophetam: ego deus, et non est praeter me. qui per eundem prophetam refert quoniam matestatem meam non dabo alter’; ut omnes cum suis figmentis ethnicos excludat et haereticos, probans deum non esse qui manu artificis factus sit, nec eum qui ingenio haeretici fictus sit. non est enim deus, cui, ut sit, quaerendus est artifex. adhuc adiecit per prophetam: caelum mihi thronus est, terra autem scabellum pedum meorum: qualem mihi aedificabitis domum, aut quis locus requiei meae? ut ostendat quoniam multo magis illum templum non capit, quem mundus non capit. et haec non ad sui iactantiam, sed ad nostri scientiam refert. neque enim ipse a nobis desiderat magnitudinis gloriam, sed nobis uult religiosam, qua pater, conferre sapientiam. quique praeterea ferinos nostros animos et de agresti immanitate tumidos et abruptos ad lenitatem trahere uolens, dicit: ef super quem requiescet spiritus meus, nisi super humilem et quietum, et trementem uerba mea? ut deum aliquatenus quantus sit possit agnoscere, dum illum per spiritum collatum discit timere. qui similiter adhuc magis in notitiam nostri uolens peruenire, ad culturam sui nostros excitans animos, aiebat: ego sum dominus, qui feci lucem et creaui tenebras; ut uicissitudinum istarum quibus noctes diesque moderantur non naturam nescio quam putaremus artificem, sed deum agnosceremus potius (quod erat uerius) conditorem. quem quoniam obtutu oculorum uidere non possumus, de operum magnitudine et uirtute et maiestate condiscimus: uisibilia enim ipsius, inquit apostolus Paulus, a creatura mundi per ea quae facta sunt intellecta conspiciuntur; sempiterna quoque eius uirtus et diuinitas: ut animus humanus ex manifestis occulta condiscens, de operum magnitudine, quae uideret, mentis oculis artificis magnitudinem cogitaret. de quo idem apostolus: reg? autem saeculorum immortali, inuisibili, soli deo honor et gloria, euasit enim oculorum contemplationem, qui cogitationis uicit magnitudinem: guoniam, inquit, ex ipso et per ipsum et in ipso sunt omnia, nam et imperio eius omnia, ut ex ipso sint: et uerbo eius digesta, ut per ipsum sint: et in iudicium eius recidunt uniuersa, ut dum ” ipso exspectant libertatem corruptione deposita, in ipsum uideantur esse reuocata.
pass_a_gloss: We therefore recognize and know this God, creator of all things, Lord, because of power, and Father because of institution: this one, I say, who spoke and all things were made; He commanded and all things came forth; about whom it is written: you made all things in wisdom; about whom Moses says: God is in heaven above and on earth below; who, according to Isaiah, measured the heaven with a palm and the earth with a fist; who looks at the earth and makes it tremble; who holds the circle of the earth and those who dwell in it like locusts; who weighs the mountains in a balance and the forests in a scale, that is, with a certain examination of divine disposition; and, lest the greatness of the earth fall into ruin unevenly lying, if it had not been balanced with equal weights, He moderately equalized this burden of earthly mass. who says through the prophet: I am God, and there is no one besides me. who through the same prophet says that He will not give His glory to another; so that He may exclude all gentiles with their figments and heretics, proving that God is not one who is made by the hand of an artisan, nor one who is invented by the mind of a heretic. for He is not God, for whom, in order to exist, an artisan is sought. He added further through the prophet: heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool of my feet; what kind of house will you build for me, or what place of rest for me? so that He may show that the temple does not contain Him, whom the world does not contain. and He says these things not for His own boasting, but for our knowledge. for He Himself does not desire glory of greatness from us, but wants to impart religious wisdom to us, as a Father. and who, furthermore, wanting to draw our savage minds and those swollen with rustic barbarity and roughness to gentleness, says: but upon whom will my Spirit rest, if not upon the humble and quiet and those who tremble at my words? so that one may be able to recognize what kind of God He is, while learning to fear Him through the Spirit bestowed. who, similarly, wanting to come to our knowledge even more, exciting our minds to the cultivation of Himself, was saying: I am the Lord, who made light and created darkness; so that we may not think that some nature is the artisan of these alternations by which nights and days are moderated, but rather recognize God, the creator (which is truer). whom, since we cannot see with the eyes of our sight, we learn from the greatness and power and majesty of His works: for the visible things of Him, says the apostle Paul, are understood and seen through the things that have been made, from the creation of the world; also His eternal power and divinity: so that the human mind, learning hidden things from manifest ones, may think of the greatness of the artisan from the magnitude of the works that it sees. about whom the same apostle says: now to the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, to the only God be honor and glory; for He has escaped the contemplation of the eyes, who has overcome the magnitude of thought: because, he says, all things are from Him and through Him and in Him; for all things are by His command, so that they may be from Him; and all things are arranged by His word, so that they may be through Him; and all things return to His judgment, so that, while they await freedom, having laid aside corruption, they may seem to have been recalled to Him.

pass_b_english: We therefore acknowledge and know this God as the Creator of all things, as Lord on account of his power, and as Father on account of his governance. He spoke, and all things came into being; he commanded, and the universe proceeded forth. Scripture says of him, 'You made all things in wisdom' (Psalm 104:24). Moses declares, 'God is in heaven above and on the earth beneath' (Deuteronomy 4:39). According to Isaiah, he measured the heavens with a palm's breadth and the earth with his fist (Isaiah 40:12). He looks at the earth, and it trembles (Psalm 104:32). He holds the circle of the earth, and its inhabitants are like grasshoppers (Isaiah 40:22). He weighs the mountains in a balance and the forests in a scale—that is, by a precise examination of divine ordering. Moreover, lest the earth's vast mass, unevenly spread, collapse into ruin, he balanced it with equal weights and so moderately stabilized this burden of earthly matter. Through the prophet he says, 'I am God, and there is no other besides me' (Isaiah 45:5). Through the same prophet he declares that he will not give his glory to another (Isaiah 42:8); thus he excludes all Gentiles with their fabrications and all heretics, proving that God is not an artifact made by an artisan's hand, nor a fiction invented by a heretic's mind. For that is not God for whom an artisan must be sought in order to exist. He added further through the prophet: 'Heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool of my feet; what kind of house will you build for me, and what place will be my rest?' (Isaiah 66:1-2). He says this to show that the temple cannot contain him whom the world cannot contain. He speaks these things not for his own boasting but for our knowledge. He himself does not desire glory of greatness from us; rather, as a Father he wishes to impart to us religious wisdom. Furthermore, desiring to draw our savage minds—swollen with rustic barbarity and roughness—toward gentleness, he says: 'But upon whom will my Spirit rest, if not upon the humble and quiet and those who tremble at my words?' (Isaiah 66:2). He does this so that one may be able to recognize how great God is, while learning to fear him through the Spirit bestowed. Similarly, desiring to come even more fully into our knowledge, and stirring our minds to cultivate him, he was saying: 'I am the Lord, who made light and created darkness' (Isaiah 45:7)—so that we might not suppose some unknown nature to be the artisan of these alternations by which nights and days are governed, but rather recognize God as the Creator, which is the truth. Since we cannot see him with our physical eyes, we learn his greatness, power, and majesty from his works. For, as the apostle Paul says, his invisible attributes—his eternal power and divine nature—have been clearly perceived ever since the creation of the world, understood through the things that have been made (Romans 1:20). Thus the human mind, learning hidden things from manifest ones, may contemplate the greatness of the Artisan from the magnitude of the works it sees. Concerning him the same apostle declares: 'Now to the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever' (1 Timothy 1:17). He has escaped the contemplation of the eyes, having surpassed the magnitude of thought. For, Paul says, all things are from him and through him and in him (Romans 11:36). All things exist by his command, so that they may be from him; all things are ordered by his word, so that they may be through him; and all things fall under his judgment, so that—while they await freedom, having laid aside corruption—they may appear to have been recalled to him.

review.notes: The translation accurately reflects the Latin text. Pass A provides a faithful clause-by-clause translation. Pass B provides a more fluent version with necessary scripture citations (e.g., Psalm 104:24 for 'omnia in sapientia fecisti', Isaiah 40:12 for 'mensus est caelum palmo', Romans 1:20 for 'uisibilia enim ipsius... apostolus Paulus', etc.) which are required for patristic texts. The OCR error 'dzx7t' in the source is handled by the translator's choice 'spoke' based on context ('et facta sunt omnia'). The OCR error 'matestatem' is handled as 'glory'.
